course_description:
The course gives a broad practical understanding of processes of group development and function including understanding team roles, personal interactions in groups, leadership and conflict management.

Working effectively in groups and teams is one of the most valued capabilities in modern professional life, and nowhere more so than in the agrifood food, natural resource management, and sustainability sectors. Industry partners consistently tell the University of Queensland that these are the skills your future employers most want to see in graduates. This course builds your understanding and practical skills in working with groups and teams early in your program of study. You will explore how individuals differ in the way they communicate, process information, and approach learning, and how those differences shape collaborative decision-making. You will examine how groups form, function, and fail, and develop practical skills in facilitation, consensus building, conflict management, and negotiation. You will also explore how leadership is developed and shared in collaborative settings.

As the course is offered through the School of Agriculture and Food Sustainability, examples and case studies draw on contexts from agribusiness, rural development, food systems sustainability, food, agriculture and animal sciences, natural resource management, and sustainability. However, the knowledge and skills developed in the course are broadly applicable to students from a wide range of disciplines and professional fields.

At the School of Agriculture and Food Sustainability, we are committed to creating an inclusive and empowering learning environment for all students. We value and respect the diverse range of experiences our students bring to their education, and we believe that this diversity is crucial for fostering a rich culture of knowledge-sharing and meaningful exploration. We hold students and staff accountable for actively contributing to establishing a respectful and supportive learning environment.

Bullying, harassment, and discrimination in any form are strictly against our principles and againstﾠ UQ Policy, ﾠand will not be tolerated. If you have any concerns about your experience in this course, we encourage you to tell a member of the course teaching team. Your well-being and a positive learning atmosphere are of utmost importance to us.

assessment_details.title: Integrated Report (Group Analysis + Personal Reflection)
assessment_details.category: Paper/ Report/ Annotation, Participation/ Student contribution
assessment_details.task_description: This assessment brings together two capabilities that are often treated separately but are deeply connected in practice: the ability to analyse how a group functions, and the ability to reflect honestly on your own role within teams and groups. The best food and agricultural professionals and sustainability practitioners are not just technically competent — they can read a group situation clearly and understand what their own behaviour contributes to it. Assessment 1 is a single integrated written report with two distinct parts . Both parts must be present in your submission for it to be considered complete. The total submitted word count is 1,800–2,300 words, broken down as follows: Part A is a structured analytical report in which you select a real group from your professional or personal experience and apply course frameworks from Modules 1 and 2 to examine how the group has developed, how individual differences have shaped its communication, what dysfunction has occurred, and what specific improvements you would recommend. Part A has five required sections; see the Part A structure guide on Blackboard for the specific sections and their word allocations. Part B is a 600–800 word personal reflection written in response to three guided prompts, synthesising the thinking you have accumulated across the semester. Throughout the semester you will maintain a structured reflective journal, responding to module-linked prompts released on Blackboard at the start of each module. These prompts are designed to help you connect course content to your own experiences, observations, and developing understanding. Your journal must be attached as an appendix to this assessment document, providing evidence of your engagement with the course across the semester. Although attached to your submission, the journal itself does not receive a separate mark — it is read only in support of your Part B reflection, and there is no prescribed word length for individual journal entries. Markers will consider whether your Part B reflection is consistent with, and clearly developed from, the journal entries provided; reflections that do not draw evidently on sustained engagement across the semester will not score as highly as those that do. Part B is not a task you begin at the end of semester — it is a distillation of reflection you have been building throughout the course. The two parts are submitted as a single document. Use clear headings to separate them. Your reference list appears at the end of the document after Part B, covers both parts, and is excluded from the total word count. assessment_details.submission_guidelines:
The two parts are submitted as a single document. You must submit your Assessment task, in Blackboard, via the correct link by the submission deadline. You should also retain an electronic copy of every piece of assessment you submit.
Students with an approved extension will complete their alternative assessment in Blackboard, using the correct link.
Legal Declaration:
By submitting your work via this website, you formally declare that (1) it is your own original work, and no part of the work has been copied from any other source or person except where due acknowledgement is made; (2) no part of the work has been previously submitted for assessment in this or any other institution; and (3) you have read the Student Integrity and Misconduct Policy and understand its implications.
Deferral or extension
You may be able to apply for an extension .
The maximum extension allowed is 28 days. Extensions are given in multiples of 24 hours.
Submission of an Extension of Assessment Due Date (EADD) should be completed online through your My Requests tab via my.UQ Dashboard , in accordance with the University's Assessment Procedure (located in the Policies and Procedures section of this course profile) which outlines the requirements for requesting extensions to assessment due dates. Extensions require the correct evidence/documentation to support the requested length of time of the extension.
Late submission
A penalty of 10% of the maximum possible mark will be deducted per 24 hours from time submission is due for up to 7 days. After 7 days, you will receive a mark of 0.
For example, a report worth a maximum of 40 marks, submitted 28 hours late will attract a penalty of 8 marks, calculated as 2 periods of 24 hours x 10% x 40 marks.
Assessment deadlines are firm and must be met. Late submission without permission or non-submission of assessable work will result in penalties being applied . Late submission of assessment will only be granted for documented medical reasons, accident, bereavement, jury service and other circumstances allowed in the UQ Policies and Procedures Library (PPL).

assessment_details.title: In-person Group Facilitation Simulation — Small Groups, Individually Assessed
assessment_details.category: Participation/ Student contribution, Presentation, Role play/ Simulation
assessment_details.due_date: 16/10/2026 - 23/10/2026 In class in weeks 11 & 12. You must attend your allocated session.
assessment_details.task_description: Assessment 2 is a live, in-person facilitation exercise conducted during timetabled sessions in Weeks 11 and 12 at the Gatton campus. You must attend your allocated session. It cannot be completed online or submitted as a written task. Your scenario briefing and role card will be released on Blackboard 48 hours before your session — it is your responsibility to read these in advance. If you are unable to attend due to illness or exceptional circumstances, you must notify the course coordinator as early as possible and provide supporting documentation (such as a medical certificate). Alternative sessions will be arranged only where documentation is provided and circumstances are genuinely exceptional. Students who do not attend their allocated session without approved documentation will receive no marks for this assessment. Your performance is observed and marked in real time by the course coordinator and members of the teaching team, against a rubric covering four criteria: facilitation technique, conflict management, communication, and adaptability. See Blackboard for the full marking rubric. You will be placed in a group of 4–5 students and assigned a role in a structured, realistic scenario. One student in the group acts as the primary facilitator; the remaining students play team members with defined professional backgrounds, interests, and positions relevant to the scenario. The scenario is set in a realistic agricultural, food industry, or natural resource management context. Students will receive their scenario briefing and role card on Blackboard 48 hours before their scheduled session. Further details of the assessment will be provided in Week 2. Students are required to form their groups during Week 1. If a student has not joined or formed a group by Week 3, they should contact the course coordinator immediately so they can be placed in one. If a student has not made contact by Week 3, the course coordinator will assign them to a group in Week 4. Please note: students who do not join a group will be encouraged to withdraw from the course, as there are some assessments that are group-based. Your absence will not disadvantage other students in your group. The simulation session will proceed as planned with the remaining group members. Where a group is reduced to fewer than three students due to an approved absence, the course coordinator will make alternative arrangements for that session, which may include merging groups or rescheduling the session, or arranging for volunteers to support the group, so that all affected students can fully participate and be assessed fairly. Students who are unable to attend their allocated session due to illness or exceptional circumstances must notify the course coordinator as early as possible and provide supporting documentation. Without approved documentation, no marks can be awarded for this assessment. assessment_details.title: End-of-Semester Exam
assessment_details.task_description: Assessment 3 is a formal, closed-book, paper-based examination held in person on the UQ Gatton campus during the end-of-semester examination period. Content from all five course modules is examinable. Your exact exam date, time, and venue will be communicated by UQ Examinations and published in your personal exam timetable on my.UQ. The exam tests something that the Integrated Report and Facilitation Simulation cannot: your ability to draw on the full body of course theory independently, under individual conditions, and apply it analytically to situations you have not seen before. When a difficult group dynamic emerges on a property, in a processing plant, or at a community meeting, you will not always have time to consult notes or colleagues. What you will have is your understanding — and the exam tests exactly that. All students enrolled in this course must attend the exam in person. You are required to bring your UQ student ID card to the examination venue. This assessment task is to be completed in-person. The use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) or Machine Translation (MT) tools will not be permitted. Any attempted use of AI or MT may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. Read full task description Hide full task description
